description: Hi! I am a school student interested in space exploration and earth science. For this hackathon, I am creating a visual storytelling project about Earth locations that mimic Moon and Mars landscapes. I love graphic design and writing interesting stories. Looking forward to a great space challenge!
summary: Our project is an interactive visual tour comparing five extreme Earth environments — the Atacama Desert (Chile), Devon Island (Canada), Mauna Loa Volcano (Hawaii), Craters of the Moon lava tubes (Idaho), and McMurdo Dry Valleys (Antarctica) — with their counterparts on Mars and the Moon. Using open NASA imagery and planetary data, we analyze shared geological, climatic, and environmental characteristics such as hyper-aridity, basaltic regolith, permafrost, and radiation shielding. For each location, we highlight real NASA analog missions and field tests (including ARADS, Haughton-Mars Project, HI-SEAS, BRAILLE, and Icebreaker) that prepare spacesuits, autonomous robots, and life-support systems for permanent lunar bases under the Artemis program and future human missions to Mars
details:
"Earth’s Alien Twins" is structured as a guided virtual expedition across five terrestrial analog sites that mirror surface and subsurface conditions on the Moon and Mars. Each stop consists of a visual side-by-side comparison pairing NASA orbital or rover imagery of Mars/Moon with terrestrial photography, supported by comparative data tables (temperature, precipitation, geology, and radiation/lighting conditions) and a breakdown of historical and modern NASA field tests
Testing spacesuits, cryogenic drills, and cave-mapping robots on Earth saves billions of dollars and reduces risks before launching hardware into deep space. Our guide helps students, researchers, and space enthusiasts understand why sites like lunar lava tubes and the Lunar South Pole (Shackleton Crater) are critical for building sustainable permanent bases under NASA's Artemis program
Created in Apple Keynote and exported as accessible PDF presentations, utilizing open-source planetary imagery and scientific archives from NASA
